story.hook: My neighbor was charging his scooter from me

punchline.text: The shortcut he took to save money became the most expensive charging plan in the building.

story.script:
The first clue was my electricity bill. It had jumped by almost forty percent, even though I had spent half the month traveling for work. I checked the air-conditioning timer, the water heater, every appliance I could think of. Nothing explained it.

Then one Saturday morning, I opened my front door and found an extension cable running from the weatherproof socket beside my shoe cabinet, across the shared corridor, and into my neighbor's parking bay downstairs. The cable was plugged into his electric scooter charger.

I knocked on his door and asked how long he had been using my socket. He looked genuinely surprised that I cared. He said the outlet was outside, so he assumed it was common property. I pointed out that it was physically attached to my meter and had my unit number printed above it. He shrugged and said it could only cost a few dollars.

I unplugged the cable and asked him not to use it again. He agreed.

Two nights later, my smart-home app sent an alert that the outdoor socket had switched on at 2:13 a.m. I had installed a smart relay months earlier because delivery riders sometimes needed the corridor light. I opened the energy history. There were overnight spikes going back eleven weeks, almost always between midnight and five in the morning.

The next morning, the extension cable was back.

This time I didn't touch it. I took photos, exported the energy log, and emailed building management asking whether the socket was private. They replied that it was part of my unit and that running an unattended cable across a shared escape route was also a safety violation.

My neighbor got angry when management contacted him. He came over with a calculator and offered me twenty dollars to “settle the misunderstanding.” According to my relay, his charging sessions had used more than six times that amount. I told him I wasn't looking to profit. I wanted the charging to stop and the actual electricity reimbursed.

He refused the calculation and said my smart relay couldn't prove his scooter used the power.

That argument lasted until management checked the corridor camera. The footage didn't show inside either home, but it clearly showed him carrying the same orange extension cable from my socket to his scooter on dozens of nights.

Management issued him a written warning. They also required him to remove the cable immediately because of the trip hazard. He reimbursed the exact metered cost, down to the cent, through the management office.

I thought that would be the end of it.

A week later, he knocked on my door holding a small gift bag. Inside was a proper charging adapter for the outlet in his own parking bay. He apologized and admitted he had known my socket wasn't communal. His bay's outlet needed a paid activation, and he had been trying to avoid the fee.

I thanked him for finally being straight with me, but I still disabled my outdoor socket when I wasn't using it.

The funniest part came the next month. Building management sent every resident a notice about private electrical outlets and safe charging. My neighbor had complained that the rules were unclear, so management attached a diagram showing his exact parking bay and the correct outlet.

He had spent eleven weeks borrowing my electricity to avoid an activation fee that was cheaper than what he eventually reimbursed me.

The shortcut he took to save money became the most expensive charging plan in the building.
